answer.decision: Choose continuous transaction-log backups plus weekly full backups, lifecycle tiering for older backups, and regular restore testing.
answer.action: Capture and durably store transaction logs at least every 15 minutes; create weekly full database backups; retain 12 month-end recovery points for 12 months; tier older eligible backups to cold storage; automate backup-chain validation; and run quarterly restore drills that include cold-tier retrieval. Before rollout, model total storage and retrieval costs to confirm at least a 35% monthly reduction, then monitor cost, RPO, and RTO compliance.
reasons: Log backups taken at least every 15 minutes can meet the 15-minute RPO.
The demonstrated weekly-full-plus-logs restore took 76 minutes; even adding the stated maximum 20-minute cold retrieval delay yields 96 minutes, within the 120-minute RTO.
Replacing daily fulls addresses the backup category responsible for 72% of current storage cost, while cold tiering reduces eligible per-GB cost by 68%.
Compliance requires 12 months of month-end recoverability, not one year of daily full images.
Thirty-day retention would violate the compliance requirement, while retaining daily fulls relies on unproven negotiated pricing to meet the cost target.
Document storage is already lifecycle-tiered, making database backup policy the principal remaining cost lever.
assumptions: Transaction logs can be captured, replicated, and retained at intervals no greater than 15 minutes.
The 76-minute restore result remains representative of production data volume and infrastructure.
Month-end recovery points can be preserved as independently restorable fulls or validated full-and-log chains.
The cost model includes log growth, retained month-end recovery points, cold-tier retrieval fees, and temporary restore storage.
risks: Missing or corrupted logs could break recovery chains; automated validation and restore drills are required.
Cold-tier retrieval could consume RTO margin, particularly if delays exceed the stated 20-minute maximum.
Production data growth or retrieval charges could prevent the required 35% savings despite lower stored volume.
Weekly fulls increase dependence on longer log chains compared with daily fulls.
The available evidence strongly supports substantial savings but does not itself prove the final monthly reduction without workload-specific pricing and retention calculations.

citations.claim: Database RPO is at most 15 minutes, database RTO is at most 2 hours, and monthly backup storage cost must fall by at least 35%.
Daily full database backups account for 72% of current backup storage cost.
Point-in-time recovery logs average 6% of one daily full backup's storage per day.
Compliance requires 12 months of month-end recoverability but does not require daily full images.
A weekly-full-plus-logs restore completed in 76 minutes.
Cold storage costs 68% less per GB and can add up to 20 minutes of retrieval delay.
Document objects already use lifecycle tiering, so database backups are the dominant remaining cost lever.
